**The idea, in a paragraph.** Hybrid's checker *reconstructs* ownership from syntax: shape inference guesses which bindings share backing storage, alias/share graphs link copies, loan windows track `&m[k]`, freeze-on-move propagates through peers, and closure bodies are walked frame by frame. Every seam of the language reopens that reconstruction — and we have the receipts: in a single day, four of our reports landed as merged soundness fixes (#110 closure captures missing from freeze, #111 A3 events crossing callee frames/share-peers/closure call sites, #123 E3006 missing closure bodies + const copies + `delete`, and the earlier #44/#37 const writes), each one extending the same analysis *one more frame*. The proposal: stop inferring and start *stating*. (a) **Linear capability types on the Hybrid surface** — `own[T]`, `share[T]`, `view[T]` — where `move` consumes a capability *in the type*, and a copy/alias/rebind that would share storage is a type error instead of a graph fact. A closure that captures `own[T]` either consumes it once or does not typecheck; there is nothing left to "walk". (b) **One runtime ownership bit per composite header** (an atomic flag flipped at move/send/boundary-cross), so even the ambient reaches a reconstruction missed — a `const`/`let` copy that somehow aliases moved state — still fails closed at the boundary. The guarantee strengthens from "accepted ⇒ proven by reconstruction" to "accepted ⇒ typed-linear locally + dynamically double-checked at the boundary".

**Which assumption it breaks.** The ownership model's *epistemology*: that soundness can be reached by extending a local, syntax-directed analysis frame by frame. It also kills the A5 perimeter doctrine ("flatten/uses/calls never descend into FnLit bodies") — that doctrine is a *consequence* of reconstruction (you skip what you cannot afford to re-analyze); with capabilities there is nothing to re-analyze. Secondary casualty: the claim in practice that "reads stay legal" — under linearity, reading through a moved-out `own[T]` is a type error, not a missed check.

**Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment.** A feature bounty pays for the next patch on the reconstruction machine, and the patch queue never closes: #109 → #111 → #123 were three seams of the same day, and the tracker shows siblings still open (#92, #98, #105, #114 — every one of them "analysis missed a frame"). This proposal is the indictment of the patching pattern itself: the facts the analysis chases (who owns which backing array) are exactly the facts types can carry and a single runtime bit can verify — reconstructing them from shapes is accidental complexity, and its error surface grows with every grammar feature the community keeps asking for (Discussion #18). What changes about what Hybrid *is*: from "Go plus a checker that proves your sharing" to "Go plus a linear overlay where sharing is explicit syntax". Trust base shrinks (linearity is local, per-function, decidable), the guarantee gets strictly stronger (the runtime bit covers the residual ambient reaches that defeated us), and the `managed` hatch shrinks toward true FFI/interop only. Plain-Go emit survives untouched — the sacred cow that should live is the one that dies.

**How we would know it works (or doesn't).** Three pre-registered kill criteria, then one constructive milestone:

1. **Overhead.** G2-style bench (map/slice-heavy single-task paths from the corpus + examples): median regression >5% on the runtime bit alone → dead, publish as M2 learning.
2. **Expressiveness.** ≥30% of corpus 42 (or the examples) cannot be typed in the capability surface without inventing a *new open escape hatch* → dead (we would have moved the hole, not closed it).
3. **Adoption bar.** The "add one `.hy` file beside your `.go` and nothing else changes" pitch dies because capabilities must leak into plain-Go signatures at module scale → dead.

**Constructive milestone (the sharpest test):** retype corpus rows 21–30 (the A1c/A1b/A3 family — the exact programs our four PRs had to teach the analyzer) as capability-typed variants that reject #109/#111/#123-shaped programs *with the freeze/loan/closure frames deleted, not extended*. If linearity rejects what the reconstruction machine needed four patches to catch, the reconstruction era should end, and MOONSHOT.md gets either the beginning of that end or a published wall with numbers.

**Cost honesty.** This deletes the bridge's brain: `freeze.rs` / `loans.rs` / `closures.rs` collapse into a linearity pass plus one boundary-emit hook (~the checker's core, not its edge). Needs a small parser/type surface for the capability wrappers (no Go-generics dependency required — they can be nominal wrappers the emitter erases). The runtime bit needs an ABI convention for composite headers (one word, atomic ops at move/send only) — runtime/bridge changes included. Migration = retyping the 42-row corpus + three months of docs that teach capabilities instead of "how the checker thinks". Emit stays plain Go. The honest headline: **this deletes the alias/loan/freeze analysis as a product surface and rewrites the checker core** — which is exactly the kind of answer the cost field asks for.

*Terms: both boxes understood — failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome (M2), and all outcomes, including a decline, are published in MOONSHOT.md. Submitted by `zidirahim617-del` (Hall of Fame: #44/#37, #46, #26; this cycle's merged soundness landings: #102, #110, #117, #126) — the evidence above is our own bug history, not a thought experiment.*

title: [wildcard] Make hy-emit untrusted: independently validated lowering to plain Go

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Make `hy-emit` an **untrusted producer**, rather than part of the safety argument: each checked function produces ordinary Go plus a candidate correspondence certificate, and a separate translation validator checks the *actual generated Go* against a small, explicitly specified checked-effect IR. The certificate is only a hint, never evidence by itself. The validator independently reconstructs the Go control-flow graph and verifies a simulation relation, including effect order and loan store-back obligations. Missing correspondence, unsupported constructs, or changed output fail closed for certification. Keep `.hy`, the ownership checker, and readable Go; change the accepted compilation artifact from "checker verdict + generated text" to "checker verdict + independently validated lowering." This is a research proposal, not a claim that such a validator exists or that current lowering is unsound.

### Which assumption it breaks

It attacks the assumption that trusting the frontend/checker requires trusting its emitter too. At inspected main commit `00610f758cec696b53347ef9199b875d308e48b4`, [stmt.rs](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/00610f758cec696b53347ef9199b875d308e48b4/compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/stmt.rs) explicitly drops `move` markers for sends, lowers `task` to a plain goroutine, and emits `managed` as a block with an audit comment. Those are intentional lowering choices, not bugs identified by this submission. They make the distinction between a checked source property and preservation of that property across lowering worth making explicit.

The proposal does **not** remove `hy-check` from the trusted base or prove arbitrary foreign Go safe. The initial IR and its connection to checked source must have a written semantics and an independently reviewed adequacy argument; merely serializing the emitter's decisions would be circular. Go parsing/type resolution, the validator's semantic rules, and the downstream Go compiler/runtime remain trust assumptions.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

The architectural bet is to decouple safety acceptance from code-generation implementation. A future emitter rewrite or optimization would be permitted to search for code freely, but would have to discharge the same independently checked preservation obligations. This is not another AST-walker patch or an extra `go build` check: a type-correct output can still reorder an observable effect.

Related proposals, and the intended distinction:

- #174 encodes ownership witnesses into Go's type system and also proposes a second checker oracle. This proposal keeps the existing checker, avoids phantom/CPS encoding, and targets **translation equivalence**, including observable effect order, rather than using Go type-checking as an ownership proof.
- #186 replaces the `.hy` frontend/emitter with native Go analysis. This proposal keeps that split and validates the boundary between them.
- #304 changes the ownership model to region capabilities. This proposal does not change ownership semantics.

Translation validation is an established idea; I am not claiming global novelty. The proposed experiment is whether its trust-boundary inversion is useful for Hybrid's specific lowering rules. If maintainers consider it subsumed by #174, a shared evaluation or decline is preferable to duplicating that work.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Before implementing anything, pin a commit and publish an inventory and hashes of the selected source cases, output cases, and mutations. Do not assume today's corpus count is fixed.

1. Specify a bounded subset: single-function straight-line control flow, branches and loops with explicit invariants, map-slot loan store-back, and return/break/continue. Calls must have explicit effect summaries or be treated as ordered opaque events. Unknown constructs are unsupported, not silently widened to `managed`.
2. Define the source-to-IR adequacy assumptions and the IR-to-Go simulation obligations. Model normal exits and exceptional exits explicitly; if panic/defer cannot yet be modeled, reject those cases from certification and report the coverage loss. Concurrency and foreign/managed internals are outside the initial equivalence claim; a later extension must model their traces before certifying them.
3. Prototype an independent checker over the actual typed Go CFG. Certificates map source/IR states to output states and provide invariants; the checker verifies transition obligations, rather than trusting annotations or sharing the emitter's walker. Bind checked IR, exact Go bytes, dependency/effect summaries, and validator version by digest. Reject missing paths, stale certificates, or changed checked/managed boundaries.
4. Try mutations that remain Go-type-correct: drop a required store-back, reorder a store-back across an effectful call, duplicate an effect, and redirect an exit. Every non-equivalent mutation must fail validation. Positive cases must preserve their specified traces; tests are a falsification aid, not proof of the semantic rules.
5. Publish supported/unsupported counts against the *pre-registered* inventory, validator size, compile-time overhead, counterexamples, and the trust assumptions. The proposed feasibility bar is at least 90% of the agreed positive subset and rejection of every non-equivalent mutation. Coverage achieved by weakening the contract does not pass. A demonstrated semantic wall is a useful failure result.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

This needs a new specified IR, a verifier, and source/output mappings. It can easily become a second compiler. Start with a bounded design-and-falsification spike, not a production rewrite. If independent validation requires reconstructing essentially all emitter logic, cannot handle exit/effect ordering soundly, or only accepts a toy subset, publish that failure and stop the architectural claim. No zero-overhead, whole-program equivalence, or proof of checker correctness is promised. Production integration would be a separate reviewed decision.

### Track terms

- [x] I understand no prototype is required and failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome under the track's acceptance and publication conditions.
- [x] I understand all outcomes, including declines and failures, are published in MOONSHOT.md.

Submitted for Wildcard Track consideration only. The advertised $250 acceptance / $250 published-learning milestones are not an award or payment claim. No prototype or benchmark has been run for this proposal.

title: [$400] Per-service container images: ship each image only the code and dependencies it runs

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: Cash bounty paid after merge; terms in the issue

body:
## Context

SpaceApp publishes three images from one `Dockerfile`: `spaceapp-core` (API, web server, Temporal worker), `spaceapp-cli` (the CLI host that runs the AI coding CLIs in PTYs) and `spaceapp-browser` (Browser Host plus Chromium). All three build `FROM runtime-base`. That stage copies the **whole** monorepo output into every image: all of `node_modules` after `npm prune --omit=dev`, all of `apps/`, all of `packages/` and `agent-skills/`. So:

- the CLI image ships the API, the web app, the Temporal SDK with its native core bridge, pdfjs and `@napi-rs/canvas`, though it only runs `packages/cli-host/dist/main.js`;
- the browser image ships the CLI host, `node-pty`, the web app and the Temporal SDK, though it only runs `apps/api/dist/browser-host-main.js`;
- the core image ships the CLI host and `node-pty`, plus native prebuilds for platforms it never runs on.

Sizes in the latest Container matrix run on `main` (`scripts/container-image-size-budget.mjs`):

| Image | linux/amd64 | linux/arm64 | Budget |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| core | 1044.7 MiB | 1066.9 MiB | 1100 MiB |
| browser | 1719.9 MiB | 1735.0 MiB | 1750 MiB |
| cli | 1386.0 MiB | 1237.1 MiB | 2800 MiB |

The browser image is 15 MiB from its budget. The core budget already had to be raised for 1.1.5, and [`KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md`](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md) (EXT-C-F20) names the core image size as the reason some functionality cannot be added to core. Every user downloads these images on install and on every `update`.

## Goal

Each image contains only what its service runs, on both architectures, with no change in behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each target gets its own production dependency closure, for example a per-target build stage that installs only the workspaces that target runs, or a pruned deploy directory per entrypoint. Shared layers stay shared where it helps the total download.
- [ ] Measured with `scripts/container-image-size-budget.mjs` on **both** `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`:
  - core at most 850 MiB,
  - browser at most 1350 MiB,
  - cli at most 1000 MiB.

  The budgets in the script and its test (`scripts/tests/container-image-size-budget.test.mjs`) are lowered to the new sizes plus a small margin, with the measurements recorded in the comment as today.
- [ ] No functional change. Each image keeps its entrypoint, the non-root `spaceapp` user (uid/gid 10001), the healthcheck, `/app/deploy/docker/*` scripts, the `*-vscode-parity` wrapper links, OpenCode in the CLI image, `LICENSE`/`NOTICE`/`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, the owner and backup scripts in core, and the security patches applied to npm in `runtime-base`.
- [ ] Smoke checks in `.github/workflows/containers.yml` for every target and architecture, so a missing module fails CI instead of an install:
  - core starts against a pgvector PostgreSQL service, runs migrations and answers `/readyz` with `ok: true`;
  - cli starts the CLI host and accepts a connection on its socket;
  - browser starts the Browser Host and launches headless Chromium once.
- [ ] Full-stack check with the launcher on Linux: build the three images locally, tag them as the version the launcher expects, run `install --profile large`, and confirm that an OpenCode pane starts and a browser pane opens a page. Put the steps and output in the PR.
- [ ] The security workflow's image scans (`.github/workflows/security.yml`) and the release workflow (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) still pass. `scripts/tests/public-docker-distribution.test.mjs` and `scripts/tests/public-compose-config.test.mjs` are updated where they assert the Dockerfile layout.
- [ ] The README's disk requirements are updated if the smaller images change them.

## How to test

```sh
for target in core browser cli; do
  docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 --target "$target" -t "spaceapp-local:$target-amd64" --load .
  node scripts/container-image-size-budget.mjs --target "$target" --image "spaceapp-local:$target-amd64"
done
# repeat with --platform linux/arm64 (QEMU), as .github/workflows/containers.yml does
node --test scripts/tests/*.test.mjs
```

Then run the smoke checks above and a launcher install against the local images.

## Out of scope

- Changing the base image (Debian trixie slim with Node 22), the Node version or the Chromium source.
- Moving features between services, for example moving OpenCode into core (EXT-C-F20 describes that trade-off).
- Removing tools the services use at runtime (`git`, `ripgrep`, `postgresql-client`, `sqlite3`, `gosu`, ...) unless the PR shows the target never calls them.

## Pointers

- `Dockerfile` (stages `build`, `runtime-base`, `core`, `browser`, `cli`)
- `deploy/docker/core-entrypoint.sh`, `deploy/docker/core-supervisor.mjs` (core runs `apps/api/dist/server.js`, `apps/worker/dist/worker.js`, `apps/web/server.mjs` and `packages/db/dist/migrate.js`), `deploy/docker/cli-entrypoint.sh`, `deploy/docker/browser-entrypoint.sh`
- `scripts/container-image-size-budget.mjs`, `.github/workflows/containers.yml`
- `packages/run-spaceapp/templates/compose.yml` (how the images are run)
- Before opening a PR, run the checks in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#checks-before-a-commit).

title: [$750] WebGL renderer for the 3D memory graph: 50,000 nodes at interactive frame rates

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: Cash bounty paid after merge; terms in the issue

body:
## Context

The Memory workspace has a 3D view of the memory graph (files, memory records, topics and their relations). It is one of SpaceApp's most visible features. Today it does not scale:

- **Rendering** (`apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/MemoryGraph3D.tsx`) uses Canvas 2D. Every frame it projects every node on the CPU, sorts all nodes by depth, strokes every edge as its own path and draws every node with `arc()`. Hover and click hit-testing is a linear scan.
- **Layout** (`layoutMemoryNetwork3D` in `memory-3d.ts`, run in `memory-network-layout.worker.ts`) is a fixed 180-step force simulation with a hash-map spatial grid that is rebuilt each step. It finishes before anything is drawn.
- **Data**: the overview endpoint (`GET /api/admin/memory/graph/overview` in `apps/api/src/memory-graph-routes.ts`) returns at most 2,000 nodes (`selectOverviewNodes`) and 6,000 edges. It sets `truncated: true` beyond that, so larger memories are only ever shown as a sample.

Long-running workspaces easily pass 2,000 nodes, and they are the users who get the most out of the memory graph.

## Goal

The 3D view renders and interacts smoothly with **50,000 nodes and 150,000 edges**, and lets the user load the full graph instead of a 2,000-node sample.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A WebGL2 renderer replaces the Canvas 2D drawing in the 3D view: instanced nodes, batched edges, depth handled by the GPU (no per-frame CPU sort of all nodes), and colors, sizes and focus/neighbor highlighting matching the current look.
- [ ] Picking (hover and click) takes at most 4 ms at 50k nodes, using GPU picking or a spatial index (no linear scan per pointer move).
- [ ] Labels: the current rules stay (core and source labels first, collision avoidance, the `showTitles` toggle), now with level-of-detail. At most a bounded number of labels are measured and drawn per frame, whatever the graph size.
- [ ] Layout runs in the existing Web Worker, incrementally: positions stream to the main thread while the simulation converges, and the view can be used during layout. No main-thread long task over 100 ms during load or layout at 50k nodes. The output is deterministic for the same input, as it is today (`apps/web/tests/memory-3d.test.ts`).
- [ ] Data: the 3D view can request more than 2,000 nodes. One option is a `limit` parameter on the overview endpoint with a hard server maximum (at least 50,000) and the default left unchanged. Another is a paged or compact endpoint. Labels keep going through the existing redaction (`redactedNode`). The route stays admin-only. Response size and server time at 50k nodes are measured and reported in the PR.
- [ ] Performance at 50k nodes / 150k edges on a laptop with an integrated GPU (state the hardware in the PR): p95 frame time at most 33 ms while rotating and zooming. At the current 2,000-node size: p95 at most 16.7 ms. Attach the measurement (a Chrome performance trace or a small frame-time harness).
- [ ] Fallback: without WebGL2, or after a context loss, the view falls back to the current Canvas 2D renderer (with the current 2,000-node cap) and keeps working. A lost context is restored when the browser allows it.
- [ ] Accessibility stays as it is: keyboard rotation and zoom, focusable canvas, `aria-label`, `aria-busy` while loading, and the existing `data-*` attributes tests rely on (`data-rotation`, `data-layout-volume`, `data-titles-visible`).
- [ ] Demo mode (`/demo-workspace`, `apps/web/src/demo/DemoStore.ts`) can generate a synthetic graph of a given size, so anyone can reproduce the benchmark without a backend or embeddings provider.
- [ ] Unit tests for the pure parts (camera/projection math, picking, label LOD selection, layout streaming) and API tests for the new limit or endpoint (`apps/api/tests/memory-graph-api.test.ts`). Existing web and API tests pass.
- [ ] No new rendering dependency (three.js, regl, deck.gl, ...) unless it is proposed and agreed in this issue first. WebGL2 is enough for points and lines.

## How to test

```sh
ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1 npm ci
npm run check
npm test -w @space/web -- memory
npm test -w @space/api -- memory-graph
npm run dev:web     # then open http://127.0.0.1:4911/demo-workspace, open Memory, switch to 3D
```

Use the synthetic demo graph at 2k, 10k and 50k nodes. Rotate, zoom, hover and click nodes, toggle titles, and record frame times. Repeat with WebGL disabled (`chrome://flags` or `--disable-webgl`) to check the fallback.

## Out of scope

- The 2D map (`DesktopMemoryGraph.tsx`, sigma.js).
- Changes to how memory is indexed, embedded or stored, or to the graph's node and edge types.
- VR/XR, screenshots or export of the graph.

## Pointers

- `apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/MemoryGraph3D.tsx` (renderer, camera input, hit testing)
- `apps/web/src/features/memory-workspace/memory-3d.ts` (`layoutMemoryNetwork3D`, `projectMemoryPoint`, camera), `memory-network-layout.worker.ts`, `memory-network-layout.ts`

title: [$400] Test every Temporal workflow on a real time-skipping test server and gate replay determinism in CI

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: Cash bounty paid after merge; terms in the issue

body:
## Context

SpaceApp runs its long-lived orchestration on Temporal (`apps/worker`): Room Agent supervision, chat turns, Dot goals and memory maintenance. These workflows use signals, `condition()` timeouts, `continueAsNew`, child workflows and `patched()` branches. Their tests mock `@temporalio/workflow` (for example `apps/worker/tests/room-supervisor-continuation.test.ts`), so the real workflow sandbox, timers, signal ordering and continue-as-new are never exercised. Nothing checks replay determinism automatically either: a workflow change that breaks running executions would first show up in a user's installation.

This is finding **CORE-006** in [`docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md`](https://github.com/oll4com/spaceapp/blob/main/docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md): "No TestWorkflowEnvironment or time-skipping tests" and "The check is manual; it is not wired into deploy or CI".

Workflows in scope (all in `apps/worker/src`):

- `workflows.ts`: `dotGoalWorkflow`, `dummyTurnWorkflow`, `codexAppServerTurnWorkflow`, `roomAgentSupervisorWorkflow` (both the current branch and the pre-patch branch behind `patched("room-background-continuation-v1")`), `roomAgentActionWorkflow`
- `memory-maintenance-workflows.ts`: `memoryMaintenanceWorkflow`, `memoryConsolidationWorkflow`
- `memory-mutation-workflows.ts`: `memoryMutationWorkflow`

## Goal

Run every workflow in the real Temporal workflow sandbox on `@temporalio/testing`'s time-skipping environment with stubbed activities, and fail CI when a workflow change is not replay-compatible with recorded histories.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `@temporalio/testing` is a devDependency of `apps/worker`, pinned to the same version as the other `@temporalio/*` packages (1.24.0 today), with `package-lock.json` updated in the same commit.
- [ ] Each of the 8 workflows above has tests that run in a `TestWorkflowEnvironment.createTimeSkipping()` worker with the real workflow code (`workflowsPath`) and stub activities. No network, database, Docker or AI provider is needed.
- [ ] The tests cover at least:
  - `dotGoalWorkflow`: wake signal vs. timeout, and continue-as-new while the goal is unfinished;
  - `roomAgentSupervisorWorkflow`: enqueue and stop signals, the 1-second polling `condition()` loops, interrupting a running mission, continue-as-new after 50 processed items or 250 polls with the carried state intact, for both the current and the pre-patch branch;
  - `roomAgentActionWorkflow`: the `room-background-action-failure-v1` failure path;
  - `memoryMaintenanceWorkflow`: it continues when the all-months refresh or session reconciliation fails, and it runs `memoryConsolidationWorkflow` as a child;
  - activity failures and retries for the turn and memory workflows.
- [ ] Everything asserted in `room-supervisor-continuation.test.ts` is also covered by a real-sandbox test. The mocked test may stay, but it is no longer the only coverage.
- [ ] Replay gate: a script (for example `npm run temporal:record-histories -w @space/worker`) records histories from the test runs into `apps/worker/tests/fixtures/workflow-histories/` (JSON, synthetic data only). It records at least one per workflow and one that takes the pre-patch supervisor branch. A test replays all of them with `Worker.runReplayHistories` against the current workflow code.
- [ ] A negative test proves the gate works: a test-only workflow variant with an extra timer or activity fails replay with `DeterminismViolationError`.
- [ ] The tests run in `npm test -w @space/worker`, so `npm run test:public` and the public CI run them too. They add less than 3 minutes on GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` runner.
- [ ] Workflow behavior does not change. If the tests find a real bug, describe it in the PR. Any fix to workflow code must be replay-safe (`patched()`) and come with its own history fixture.
- [ ] A short section in `CONTRIBUTING.md` (or a README in `apps/worker/tests/fixtures/workflow-histories/`) explains how to re-record histories. It also says when re-recording is allowed: only together with a `patched()` change, never to make a failing replay pass.

## How to test

```sh
ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1 npm ci
npm run check
npm test -w @space/worker
```

To see the gate fail, add `await sleep("1 second")` at the start of `dotGoalWorkflow` and run the tests again. The replay test must fail with a determinism error that names the workflow and the history file.

## Out of scope

- Killing worker or server processes against a real Temporal server (`apps/worker/tests/support/disposable-temporal.ts` covers that separately).
- Changes to workflow logic, timeouts, retry policies or the Temporal server version.
- Activity implementations. They stay stubbed here and keep their own unit tests.

- `apps/worker/src/workflows.ts`, `apps/worker/src/memory-maintenance-workflows.ts`, `apps/worker/src/memory-mutation-workflows.ts`

- `docs/quality/KNOWN_LIMITATIONS.md` (CORE-006), `docs/quality/failure-matrix.md`
- Temporal TypeScript SDK docs: "Testing" (time-skipping `TestWorkflowEnvironment`) and "Replay" (`Worker.runReplayHistories`)

title: Serial by default: safe execution first

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

In an opt-in closed fork-join scope, make task execution safe by default. Rather than reject tasks whenever shared-data independence cannot be proved, the compiler orders possibly conflicting tasks sequentially. It runs tasks in parallel only when it can prove their data accesses are independent. Unknown means slower, not unsafe.

### Which assumption it breaks

Break the assumption that developers must prove sendability/ownership at every task boundary to make useful concurrent code compile. For a new closed scope, concurrency becomes an optimization, not an admission condition. If the scope's mutable state could escape to other goroutines, reject it.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Instead of 'prove concurrency safety first or fail', Hybrid could offer 'run correctly first, accelerate automatically'. This is not STM: no speculative writes, retries or rollback. It is not full object cloning or fixed-rate synchronous dataflow. Conflicts are ordered before work begins; only independent tasks run together.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Prototype two-task fork-join regions. Test same-map writes serialize and pass go test -race; proven independent roots overlap in time; ambiguous accesses serialize; an escaped reference is rejected; a blocking receive is rejected before scheduling. Measure overhead versus regular Hybrid. Fail the hypothesis if ownership isolation requires rebuilding the full alias checker or serial overhead is excessive.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Requires opt-in syntax, whole-region ownership checks, conservative read/write effect summaries, dependency-DAG scheduling and new diagnostics. First version excludes dynamic spawn, uncontrolled I/O, blocking calls and escaped references. Existing task semantics remain unchanged. AI-assisted proposal; no prototype or benchmarks claimed.

### Track terms

- [x] I understand no prototype is required and failure-with-knowledge is a valid, paid outcome
- [x] I understand all outcomes (including declines and failures) are published in MOONSHOT.md
